'''''Ranunculus tripartitus''''' ('''three-lobed crowfoot''') is a [[species]] of [[flowering plant]] in the [[Family (taxonomy)|family]] [[Ranunculaceae]], which grows in pools and muddy hollows in coastal parts of Europe, [[North Africa]] and [[West Asia]]. It is rare and endangered throughout its range, and is considered to be an indicator of favourable environmental conditions.

==Description==
''Ranunculus tripartitus'' is a procumbent [[annual plant|annual]] to [[perennial plant|perennial]] [[herbaceous plant]] that grows in shallow water and on exposed mud or [[peat]]. Under water it has finely divided, thread-like submerged (capillary) leaves. Floating on the surface, or growing on exposed mud, it has flat, deeply-lobed laminar leaves. Sometimes both leaf shapes are present on the same plant, but intermediate leaves are rare. The laminar leaves are [[Reniform leaf|reniform]] overall, divided more than half-way into three (rarely 5) lobes which are broadest towards the tip, and which are themselves shallowly indented (crenate) at the end. They are {{Convert|0.5-1.5|cm|abbr=on|sigfig=1}} across, with the middle lobe narrower than the side ones. The submerged leaves are {{Convert|1-4|cm|4=1|abbr=on}} long, divided up to 5 times, with sometimes as many as 90 terminal segments. The leaves are opposite or alternate along stems that can be up to {{Convert|50|cm|abbr=on}} long, with small stipules at the base of the petiole, which can be between 1 and 10 mm long. The stems and leaves are glabrous (hairless).<ref name=Stace>{{cite book |last1=Stace |first1=C.A. |title=New Flora of the British Isles |date=2019 |location=Suffolk |isbn=978-1-5272-2630-2}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last1=Poland |first1=John |last2=Clement |first2=Eric |title=The Vegetative Key to the British Flora |date=2009 |publisher=John Poland |location=Southampton |isbn=978-0-9560144-0-5}}</ref><ref name=Wiegleb>{{cite journal |last1=Wiegleb |first1=Gerhard |last2=Bobrov |first2=Alexander | last3=Galosz |first3=Joanna |title=A taxonomic account of ''Ranunculus'' section Batrachium (Ranunculaceae) |journal=Phytotaxa |date=2017 |volume=319 |issue=1 |pages=1–55 |doi=10.11646/phytotaxa.319.1.1 |url=http://publication.plazi.org/id/FFDEFFCC774DFFACFF80CB6BFFD86D68}}</ref>

The [[actinomorphic]] flowers are borne singly on long stalks ([[Pedicel (botany)|pedicels]]) from the leaf axils. Each flower has 5 [[petal]]s and 5 [[sepal]]s. The petals are white with a yellow patch towards to base, up to 4.5 mm long, and there is a small space between them. Towards the base of each petal is a small crescent-shaped [[nectar]] pit. The sepals are up to 3 mm long, green with a blue tip, and recurved towards the flower stalk. There are 5–8 stamens and numerous (more than 6) carpels. The [[Receptacle (botany)|receptacle]] is hairy.<ref>{{cite web |last1=National Museum of Wales |title=''Ranunculus tripartitus'' |url=https://naturalhistory.museumwales.ac.uk/corespecies/CMS/Resources/pdfs/Ranunculus_tripartitus/Ranunculus_tripartitus.pdf |access-date=26 February 2022}}</ref> The [[Achene|fruits]] are hairless and, as they develop, the pedicel becomes recurved.
{{Image frame|width=404|content=[[File:Ranunculus tripartitus winter.jpg|200px]] [[File:Ranunculus tripartitus fruit.jpg|200px]]|caption=Submerged capillary leaves and terrestrial laminar leaves of three-lobed crowfoot|align=center}}

==Taxonomy==
''Ranunculus tripartitus'' is included in the taxonomically difficult subgenus (or "section") ''Batrachium'' of the buttercup family, which includes all the water-crowfoots. They are aquatic or amphibious species, with white petals, transversely ridged achenes (fruits), and stipules at the base of the leaf stalk. It can be separated from other members of the section by the three-lobed laminar leaves, the petals being about twice as long as the sepals and not contiguous, the reflexed pedicel and the hairy receptacle.<ref name="Wiegleb" />

It was described by [[Augustin Pyramus de Candolle]] in 1808. The [[Type (biology)|type]] specimen, which was thought to be in [[National Museum of Natural History, France|Paris]], is missing, so the plate and description in de Candolle's "Icones Plantarum"<ref>{{cite book |last1=de Candolle |first1=Augustin |title=Icones plantarum Galliæ rariorum aut nondum delineatarum |date=1808 |location=Paris |url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/bibliography/49177}}</ref> has been designated a typotype. ''Ranunculus petiveri'' W.D.J. Koch, which was later found in Germany, and ''Batrachium lutarium'' Revel (France) are considered to be the same species.<ref name="Wiegleb" />

There are no subspecies of ''R. tripartitus'', but it does form hybrids with other species in the section, including ''[[R. omiophyllus]]'' (=''R.'' × ''novae-forestae'' S.D. Webster) (which is only known in Britain); [[Ranunculus aquatilis|common water-crowfoot]] (also only in Britain); and ''[[Ranunculus ololeucos|R. ololeucos]]'' (= ''R.'' × ''felixii'' Segret) (only in France). A key feature for the identification of hybrids is the presence of leaves that are intermediate between the capillary and laminar forms; such plants are also sterile.<ref name="Stace" /><ref name="Wiegleb" />

The [[Ploidy|chromosome number]] of ''R. tripartitus'' is 2n = 48.<ref name="Stace" />

==Distribution==
This is primarily a European plant, although it has been reported as far east as [[Turkey]] and as far south as [[Morocco]], so it is perhaps present on three continents. Owing to the difficulty of identifying species in the section ''Batrachium'', there is some uncertainty about its range. For example, the Turkish plants were recorded as ''R. kastamonuensis''. It may occur on the [[Aegean Islands]], but this is also unconfirmed.
In all parts of its range, ''R. tripartitus'' is considered to be rare and possibly endangered.<ref name="Wiegleb" />

In Britain, it was first recorded (as ''R. innominatus'') by [[Cardale Babington|C.C. Babington]] in 1848, "near [[Claremont (country house)|Claremont House]], Surrey",<ref>{{cite book |last1=Clarke |first1=W.A. |title=First Records of British Flowering Plants |date=1900 |publisher=West, Newman & Co. |location=London}}</ref> an area now known as [[Esher Commons]]. It still occurs in this part of the country. The other main populations in Britain are in the heaths of Sussex and Kent, the [[New Forest]], [[the Lizard]] peninsula, [[Pembrokeshire]] and [[Anglesey]].<ref name=Atlas>{{cite book |last1=Preston |first1=C.D. |last2=Pearman |first2=D.A. |last3=Dines |first3=T.D. |title=New Atlas of the British and Irish Flora |date=2002 |publisher=Oxford University Press |location=Oxford}}</ref> Because populations fluctuate dramatically, it is difficult to assess its conservation status. In 1962<ref>{{cite book |last1=Perring |first1=F.H. | last2=Walters |first2=S.M. |title=Atlas of the British Flora |date=1962 |publisher=Thomas Nelson and Sons Ltd. |location=Edinburgh}}</ref> it was thought to be present in 28 places (10 x 10 km squares) on the map. This had shrunk to 19 by 1987,<ref>{{cite book |last1=Stewart |first1=A. |last2=Pearman |first2=D.A. |last3=Preston |first3=C.D. |title=Scarce Plants in Britain |date=1987 |publisher=JNCC |location=Peterborough}}</ref> as low as 10 by 1999,<ref>{{cite book |last1=Wigginton |first1=M.J. |title=British Red Data Books 1 Vascular plants |date=1999 |publisher=Joint Nature Conservation Committee |location=Peterborough}}</ref> and back up to 27 by 2002.<ref name="Atlas" /> Given a Change Index<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Telfer |first1=M.G. |title=Change index: a measure of change in range size that is independent of changes in survey effort |journal=Proc. 13th Int. Coll. EIS |date=2003 |pages=107–110 |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/254912162}}</ref> of -1.09, it narrowly missed being classed as one of the 100 least successful plants in the British Isles.<ref name="Atlas" />

==Ecology==
The habitat of ''R. tripartitus'' is in shallow pools and muddy hollows in heathland. It requires high levels of moisture and light, and low levels of nutrients. In Britain it is considered an [[axiophyte]] wherever it occurs, and it has been described as a useful bioindicator in the Mediterranean region.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Lumbreras |first1=Ana |title=Bioindicator role of aquatic Ranunculus in Mediterranean freshwater habitats |journal=Aquatic Conservation |date=2013 |volume=23 |issue=4 |pages=582–593 |doi=10.1002/aqc.2327 |bibcode=2013ACMFE..23..582L |url=https://doi.org/10.1002/aqc.2327|url-access=subscription }}</ref> In the [[Doñana National Park]] in Spain, it is found in species-rich ponds of special conservation value.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Diaz-Paniagua |first1=Carmen |title=Tempora[r]y ponds from Donana National Park: a system of natural habitats for the preservation of aquatic flora and fauna |journal=Limnetica |date=2010 |volume=29 |issue=1 |pages=41–58 |doi=10.23818/limn.29.04 |hdl=11441/34396 |s2cid=245799706 |url=https://idus.us.es/bitstream/handle/11441/34396/Temporary%20ponds.pdf?sequence=3&isAllowed=y}}</ref>
Although it is typically found in coastal areas, it is not tolerant of saline conditions.<ref>{{cite web |last1=iNaturalist UK |title=Three-lobed Crowfoot |url=https://uk.inaturalist.org/taxa/335043-Ranunculus-tripartitus}}</ref> Its [[Indicator value|Ellenberg values]] in Britain are L = 9, F = 10, R = 6, N = 3, and S = 0.<ref>{{cite book|last1=Hill|first1=M.O.|last2=Mountford|first2=J.O.|last3=Roy|first3=D.B.|last4=Bunce|first4=R.G.H.|title=Ellenberg's indicator values for British plants. ECOFACT Volume 2. Technical Annex|date=1999|publisher=Institute of Terrestrial Ecology|isbn=1870393481|url=http://nora.nerc.ac.uk/6411/1/ECOFACT2a.pdf|access-date=29 May 2017}}</ref>

Disturbance, such as trampling and grazing by livestock, is an important factor in its conservation.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Scott |first1=Amanda |title=Artificial disturbance promotes recovery of rare Mediterranean Temporary Pond plant species on the Lizard Peninsula, Cornwall, England |journal=Conservation Evidence |date=2012 |volume=9 |pages=79–86 |url=http://mobile.www.conservationevidence.com/reference/pdf/4018}}</ref>

It is mainly a lowland plant, recorded only as high as {{Convert|300|m|abbr=on}} in Britain, at [[Belstone]] in Devon (by [[William Keble Martin]] in 1934).<ref>{{cite web |last1=Pearman |first1=D.A. |title=Altitudinal Limits of British Plants, 2021 |url=https://bsbi.org/altitudes}}</ref>
